values: Used mainly for inherited physical or character resemblance to a family member.
With a noun, tenir à often means to value or be attached to it; with an infinitive, it can mean to be keen or insist on doing the action.
Tomber en panne describes the transition into malfunction; être en panne describes the resulting state.
Depending on context, toujours means always or still; it can also reinforce a suggestion, as in tu peux toujours essayer.
The present participle in en arrivant normally shares its subject with the main verb: the person who arrives is also the person who calls.
Téléphoner requires à before the person called, unlike English call, which takes a direct object.
The recent past is formed with venir conjugated in the relevant tense, followed by de and an infinitive; it presents the event as having just occurred.
Formal polite imperative frequent in notices, instructions, and business correspondence; it is followed directly by an infinitive.
When the desired action has a different explicit subject, vouloir que requires the subjunctive; with the same subject, use vouloir + infinitive.
The possessive form changes with the person whose effort is requested: du mien, du tien, du sien, du nôtre, du vôtre, or du leur.
Informal second-person singular form urging someone to contribute effort or goodwill.
Toast addressed to one person with whom the speaker uses tu; the possessive pronoun refers elliptically to health.
Toast addressed either formally to one person or to several people.
it makes no difference to me
Tone determines whether the phrase sounds neutral, indifferent, or dismissive.

batch_summary: Added meaning contrasts for tenir and panne expressions, plus register and construction notes for the recent past, polite imperatives, wishes, and toasts.
